paper_title: GTR: Gated Token Recurrence for Efficient Dense Prediction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Self-attention-based vision backbones perform well on dense prediction, but the quadratic computational cost of global softmax attention limits their efficiency as image resolution increases. We introduce Gated Token Recurrence (GTR), a softmax-free recurrent vision backbone that combines gated linear attention, alternating spatial scan directions, and spatially enhanced SwiGLU blocks. GTR is distilled from a detection-specialized DINOv3 teacher using only final-layer patch-token alignment through a linear projection and squared $\ell_2$ loss, without masked-token prediction or intermediate-layer supervision. With Objects365 detector pre-training, GTR-L achieves 58.9 box AP on COCO \texttt{val2017} with 1.908\,ms median batch-one latency under compiled FP16 execution on an RTX~4090. The same backbone also transfers to instance segmentation, pose estimation, oriented detection, semantic segmentation, and monocular depth estimation. In an isolated kernel benchmark, our specialized chunkwise CUDA operator is $4.0\times$ faster than FLA v0.5.0 at 1.6K tokens on RTX~4090. TensorRT deployment on DRIVE AGX Thor achieves 2.282--8.769\,ms median batch-one latency across the evaluated models. These results show that recurrent token mixing can provide an efficient alternative to global softmax attention for high-resolution dense prediction and edge deployment. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Self-attention-based vision backbones have shown strong performance for dense prediction (Liu et al., 2026). However, the quadratic complexity of softmax attention with respect to the number of image tokens makes high-resolution processing increasingly expensive, particularly on resourceconstrained edge devices. Linear attention offers promising alternative: EfficientViT (Cai et al., 2023) demonstrates efficient on-device semantic segmentation, while ViG (Liao et al., 2025) explores gated linear recurrence for detection and segmentation. Despite this progress, developing general linear-attention backbone that performs consistently across diverse dense prediction tasks while meeting practical constraints on model size, computation, memory, and latency remains challenging. This motivates central question: can linear attention support general-purpose vision backbone that remains accurate across diverse dense prediction tasks while translating its theoretical efficiency into practical gains on edge hardware? We introduce Gated Token Recurrence (GTR), linear-complexity (in the number of image tokens) vision backbone designed to address this challenge. GTR builds on gated linear attention (GLA) (Yang et al., 2024b) with softmax-free, single-scale recurrent architecture. It maintains fixed patch grid across 12 blocks and performs one directional scan per block, cycling through four directions across depth to progressively aggregate global context. To complement this directional recurrence with explicit local spatial modeling, we introduce Spatial SwiGLU, which incorporates depthwise convolution into the value branch of SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020) to efficiently mix neighboring patches. Together, directional recurrence and Spatial SwiGLU provide complementary global and local spatial modeling while preserving linear complexity. Importantly, GTR uses single distillation objective that supervises only the final patch tokens. Unlike ViT-Linearizer (Wei & Chellappa, 2025), which combines intermediate activation matching with masked prediction, or ViT-AdaLA (Li et al., 2026b), which aligns attention modules before the final features, our approach distills only the final patch tokens. Specifically, GTR is aligned with frozen, detection-specialized DINOv3 teacher (Simeoni et al., 2025) using the same full-image input. linear projection and single squared ℓ2 loss constitute the entire distillation objective, requiring neither masking nor intermediate supervision. GTR scales across four model sizes (S, M, L, and X) and transfers to six dense prediction tasks: object detection, instance segmentation, human pose estimation, oriented object detection, semantic segmentation, and monocular depth estimation. With Objects365 detector pre-training (Shao et al., 2019), GTR-L achieves 58.9 box AP on COCO (Lin et al., 2014) val2017 at median forward-pass latency of only 1.908 ms under compiled FP16, batch-one inference on an RTX 4090. Beyond detection, GTR achieves competitive results in representative comparisons across the other five tasks using the same backbone design with task-specific heads and training recipes (Section 3.2; Appendix D). As summarized in Figure 1, GTR-S also exhibits slower growth in peak GPU memory and higher inference throughput than the softmax-attention-based EdgeCrafter-S (Liu et al., 2026) as input resolution increases, highlighting the practical advantage of linear-complexity attention for high-resolution dense prediction. Finally, we bridge architectural efficiency and real-world deployment with dedicated system optimizations. We develop specialized chunkwise CUDA operator for GLA (Yang et al., 2024b) that computes chunk summaries in parallel while propagating recurrent context through boundary-state scan. The operator achieves 4.0 speedup over FLA v0.5.0 (Yang & Zhang, 2024) at 1.6K tokens under FP16 and CUDA Graph execution on an RTX 4090. For end-to-end deployment on DRIVE AGX Thor, we further integrate fused kernels and graph transformations into TensorRT (NVIDIA, 2026). Across six tasks and four model scales, GTR achieves median FP16 batch-one latencies of 2.2828.769 ms, demonstrating its practicality for real-time dense prediction on edge hardware. In summary, our main contributions are: We introduce GTR, single-scale, linear-attention vision backbone for efficient dense prediction. GTR combines gated token recurrence with four-directional scanning across depth and Spatial SwiGLU for complementary global and local spatial modeling. We demonstrate the generality and scalability of GTR across six dense prediction tasks and four model scales. The same backbone design transfers effectively across object-level and pixel-level tasks using simple final-token distillation and task-specific adaptation. 2 Figure 2: Overview of GTR. Each backbone block combines GLA (Yang et al., 2024b) with Spatial SwiGLU, whose 3 3 depthwise convolution mixes neighboring patch tokens in the value branch. The 12-block backbone alternates two-dimensional scan directions and exposes intermediate features to lightweight three-scale projector. query-based head decodes the resulting feature pyramid. We enable practical edge deployment through specialized chunkwise CUDA operator and TensorRT integration. Across six tasks and four model scales, GTR achieves lowlatency FP16 inference on DRIVE AGX Thor, demonstrating low-latency deployment on automotive edge hardware.

All detection results are evaluated on COCO (Lin et al., 2014) val2017. For architectural ablations, each variant is independently distilled using the same teacher and image pool, followed by the same downstream training schedule. Full settings and results are provided in Appendix C.7. Distillation recipe. Table 3 compares our final-output alignment with ViT-Linearizer (Wei & Chellappa, 2025) and ViT-AdaLA (Li et al., 2026b) under the same teacher, GTR-S student, and COCO training schedule. For ViT-Linearizer, we use the best mask ratio (0.5) from sweep over 0.20.9. sections.title: 4 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented GTR, an efficient softmax-free backbone for dense prediction. GTR combines homogeneous GLA architecture with simple final-output distillation and optimized inference execution. Across object detection and five additional dense-prediction tasks, GTR achieves strong accuracy efficiency trade-off, while deployment on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor demonstrates its practicality on automotive hardware. These results show that linear attention can serve as an effective and efficient alternative to softmax attention for dense visual prediction.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Generative AI tools were used to assist with literature review, manuscript organization, language editing, interpretation and synthesis of the reported experimental results, and limited code development and debugging. Their use in result interpretation was limited to summarizing and describing trends and comparisons already present in the figures and tables. Generative AI tools were not used to generate, modify, or fabricate experimental data. All AI-assisted text and code were reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the final manuscript.

sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: Object detection with Transformers. DETR (Carion et al., 2020) formulates object detection as set prediction with Transformers, eliminating the need for separate non-maximum suppression (NMS). To address the slow convergence and high computational cost of the original DETR, series of follow-up works has been proposed (Zhu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023). RT-DETR (Lv et al., 2024) introduces hybrid encoder for real-time object detection. Building upon this framework, D-FINE (Peng et al., 2025) further enhances detection performance through fine-grained distribution refinement and self-distillation. Beyond architectural improvements, several studies have explored incorporating Vision Transformers (ViTs) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) into the DETR framework. LW-DETR (Chen et al., 2024) adopts self-supervised pre-trained ViT as the backbone, while RF-DETR (Robinson et al., 2026) combines neural architecture search with the visual foundation model DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) to strengthen feature representation. More recently, EdgeCrafter (Liu et al., 2026) improves compact ViT backbones via task-specific distillation from DINOv3 (Simeoni et al., 2025). Linear-complexity attention. Linear attention factorizes kernelized attention and exploits associativity to avoid materializing the dense token-to-token matrix, reducing complexity from O(L2) to O(L) and admitting recurrent evaluation (Katharopoulos et al., 2020). Modern linear-time recurrent families, including RetNet (Sun et al., 2023), RWKV (Peng et al., 2023a), Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2024), DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024c), and GLA (Yang et al., 2024b), enrich the recurrent state with retention, selectivity, delta-rule updates, or data-dependent gates while retaining parallel or chunkwise training forms. ViG (Liao et al., 2025) is the closest architectural precedent: it adapts GLA to vision with within-block bidirectional modeling, direction-wise gating, and local two-dimensional interaction, and provides non-hierarchical and hierarchical variants. Its fused bidirectional kernel also targets practical efficiency. GTR uses one scan per block, alternates directions across depth, and introduces local mixing in the SwiGLU channel mixer. We evaluate these choices together with detection-specialized distillation recipe and task-specific deployment. Hybrid approaches such as MambaVision (Hatamizadeh & Kautz, 2025) and SoLA-Vision (Li et al., 2026a) combine recurrent or linear mixers with softmax attention. Our hybrid ablation tests three softmax-layer placements within GTR-L. Kernel-based vision alternatives include LaplacianFormers low-rank Laplacian attention (Feng et al., 2026). GTR builds on the established GLA recurrence and chunkwise formulation (Yang et al., 2024b) and contributes fused, hardware-aware execution schedule for low-latency inference. Heterogeneous representation distillation. Cross-architecture transfer often uses several stages or complementary targets to bridge different token mixers. ViT-Linearizer combines intermediate token-affinity matching at multiple depths with Smooth-ℓ1 prediction of final teacher features at masked positions (Wei & Chellappa, 2025). ViT-AdaLA (Li et al., 2026b) first matches the output of every softmaxand linear-attention module with MSE, then aligns the final representations of the complete models with MSE, and finally performs supervised downstream fine-tuning. Attention to Mamba (Moudgil et al., 2026) first learns Hedgehog feature map through per-layer cosine output matching, uses it to initialize an adapted Mamba model, and then fine-tunes the model with next-token cross-entropy. Related Transformer-to-SSM studies likewise use staged conversion or additional architecture-specific objectives (Bick et al., 2024; 2025; Wang et al., 2024c). In the detection-specialized DINOv3-to-GLA setting studied here, we use single squared ℓ2 loss on the final output representations, without intermediate or stage-specific distillation targets and without input masking.

For each target scale, the aligned features from different semantic depths are concatenated along the channel dimension and fused by lightweight C2f module (Jocher, 2023): = Rs(Xl), {4, 8, 12}, P(s) = C2f (cid:16) Concat[ (cid:101)X(s) 4 , (cid:101)X(s) 8 , (cid:101)X(s) 12 ] (cid:17) , {8, 16, 32}. (6) This produces three-level feature pyramid {P(8), P(16), P(32)} with unified channel dimensions. Compared with heavier feature-pyramid encoders, this design keeps the encoder compact while aggregating early, middle, and late backbone representations at every detection scale. The three pyramid levels are then flattened and concatenated as the multi-scale memory for the decoder. B.2 QUERY-BASED DETECTION DECODER The decoder follows the DETR-style set prediction paradigm (Carion et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2025). Given the multi-scale features {P(8), P(16), P(32)}, we flatten and concatenate them into memory tokens: = Concat[Flatten(P(8)), Flatten(P(16)), Flatten(P(32))]. (7) Initial anchor proposals are generated from the multi-scale memory, and the top-k candidates with the highest classification responses are selected to initialize object queries. During training, we adopt grouped queries (Chen et al., 2023) by dividing detection queries into = 3 groups with shared decoder parameters. This provides denser supervision and improves query diversity, while only the primary group is used during inference.

sections.content: Datasets and metrics. For the main detector comparison, we report GTR with and without Objects365 (Shao et al., 2019) detector pre-training before COCO (Lin et al., 2014) train2017 fine-tuning. We evaluate on COCO val2017 with AP averaged over IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95, together with AP50, AP75, and AP for small, medium, and large objects. We report box AP for detection and mask AP for instance segmentation. For transfer evaluation, we report standard keypoint AP and AR on COCO val2017, and AP50 for oriented object detection on the DOTA-v1.0 test set (Xia et al., 2018). Training protocol. All models are trained on eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs. For the main comparison, the S/M/L/X backbones are initialized with the corresponding distilled GLA checkpoints, followed by pretraining of the full detectors on Objects365 for 36 epochs with global batch size of 128. We then train all four GTR scales for 30 epochs with global batch size of 32. The direct-COCO variants instead start from the output-aligned backbone and otherwise use the same scale-specific COCO fine-tuning configurations as their Objects365-pre-trained counterparts. The Objects365 and COCO stages use AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with flat-cosine learning-rate schedule and an exponential moving average; evaluation uses 640 640 inputs. Appendix D.1 reports the remaining scale-specific learning rates, augmentations, loss weights, and model configurations. Efficiency evaluation. We remeasure every detection and segmentation model in unified FP16, batch-size-one environment on single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090. Tables 7 and 8 report the minimum, arithmetic mean, and median per-image latency; all comparisons use the median. Compilation, graph capture, autotuning, and warm-up are excluded from timing. For DETR-style models, the measured latency covers the network forward pass alone; for YOLO variants that require NMS, it additionally includes CUDA NMS. Because deployment conversion, input resolution, and post-processing differ across model families, the complete protocol is specified in Appendix E.2. Training sources and data acquisition. We adopt the same eight-source training mixture used for depth training in YOLO26 (Jocher et al., 2026), comprising ARKitScenes (Baruch et al., 2021), SUN RGB-D (Song et al., 2015), DIODE (Vasiljevic et al., 2019), Hypersim (Roberts et al., 2021), TartanAir (Wang et al., 2020), Virtual KITTI 2 (Cabon et al., 2020), KITTI (Geiger et al., 2013), and pseudo-labeled ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009). To reduce storage and bandwidth overhead, we adopt source-specific acquisition strategies. For Hypersim, we download only the tonemap.jpg and depth meters.hdf5 files instead of the full 1.9 TB release, reducing the local storage footprint to approximately 11 GB. For KITTI, we retrieve the raw archives with batched HTTP range requests and keep only the color-camera streams, discarding the Velodyne point clouds, grayscale images, and OXTS records. This reduces the amount of data transferred by about 75%. Depth decoding. All depth targets are decoded as float32 arrays in meters, and values 0 are treated as invalid. For SUN RGB-D, we follow the official toolbox and recover depth through the 16-bit rotation = ((r 3) (r 13))/1000. We use the official depth bfx targets, which leave measured pixels unchanged while inpainting missing regions and therefore provide nearly dense supervision. Hypersim stores the Euclidean distance from the optical center rather than planar depth, i.e., the coordinate in camera space. Using the official 1024 768 intrinsics with focal length = 886.81 pixels, we convert each pixel to planar depth as z(u, v) = d(u, v) (cid:112)(u cx)2 + (v cy)2 + 2 , (8) where (cx, cy) is the principal point. Any resulting NaN is set to zero and thus marked invalid. KITTI depth is decoded from uint16 as = r/256, with zeros retained as invalid. For DIODE, we multiply the depth by the provided validity mask, which maps invalid pixels to zero. All depth maps are resized using nearest-neighbor interpolation only, so that invalid zeros are never blended with valid metric depths. We further apply dataset-specific preprocessing before enforcing the common training range. In Virtual KITTI 2, sky pixels are encoded with depth of 655.35 m; we clip these values to 80 while retaining them as valid. In contrast, sky depths in TartanAir are on the order of 104 m; these values are set to zero and treated as invalid. For DIODE and SUN RGB-D, depth values are clipped to 80 and 10 m, respectively. Across all datasets, training and evaluation use common maximum depth of 100 m, with depths in the range [103, 100] considered valid. Depth teacher. We generate metric-depth pseudo-labels with the nested variant of Depth Anything 3 (DA3) (Lin et al., 2026), which jointly estimates camera intrinsics and metric depth and therefore needs no additional scale calibration. The alternative canonical-depth DA3 variant instead predicts depth up to focal-length-dependent scale and must be rescaled as dmetric = (f /300) dcanonical, where is the focal length in pixels and 300 pixels is the canonical focal length used during training. This rescaling is not applicable in our setting: standard ImageNet preprocessing discards the camera metadata and resizes and crops each image, so the effective focal length cannot be recovered reliably. Estimating from an assumed field of view would inject an uncontrolled, per-image scale error into the pseudo-labels, which the nested variant avoids by construction. Batched teacher inference. The default DA3 inference pipeline assumes multi-view inputs from common scene rather than batch of independent images: it couples the views in batch through cross-view attention, shared scale alignment, and joint percentile-based depth normalization. Batching unrelated ImageNet images therefore makes each prediction depend on the other images in the batch; we measured median relative deviations of 68233% from single-image inference. To batch efficiently while preserving single-image behavior, we feed each sample as single-view input, yielding tensors of shape (B, 1, 3, H, ), and run global alignment and post-processing independently for each batch element. The resulting predictions match single-image inference to within 0.1% relative error. We further bucket images by their resolution after teacher preprocessing rather than by their original resolution, so that every batch shares single resolution while images with A12 common aspect ratios can still be grouped together. Overall, batching with resolution bucketing reduces the number of teacher forward passes by factor of approximately 8. Sampling and augmentation. The measured-depth datasets differ by more than an order of magnitude in size, ranging from roughly 10K images in SUN RGB-D to over 300K in TartanAir. To mitigate this imbalance, we oversample each dataset with an integer repetition factor, using [6, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 3] in data-loader order. The pseudo-labeled ImageNet pool is drawn from separate sampling stream, so that its ratio to the measured-depth data can be controlled independently. For augmentation, we retain only the metric-depth-preserving transformations of Depth Anything V2 (Yang et al., 2024a): color jitter, horizontal flipping, aspect-ratio-preserving shortedge resizing, and random square cropping. Composition-based geometric augmentations such as Mosaic, ZoomOut, and IoUCrop are disabled, since they alter the relationship between image scale and metric depth and thus break geometric consistency. First, we adopt angle distribution refinement (ADR) (Ding et al., 2026), which represents each oriented box by six discrete distributions: four distances to the sides of its axis-aligned enclosing box and two vertex offsets. These distributions are decoded into oriented boxes by distance-to-rotated-box conversion, which avoids the angular boundary discontinuity of direct angle regression. Second, we rotate the sampling offsets of deformable attention by the predicted angle θ of each query, so that the sampling pattern aligns with the principal direction of the target. Third, oriented contrastive denoising (OCD) (Ding et al., 2026) perturbs only the axis-aligned coordinates (x1, y1, x2, y2) of the denoising queries and leaves the angle channel unchanged. For classification, the matching-aware loss (MAL) (Huang et al., 2025b) uses soft target weighted by the rotated IoU with the ground truth. sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Scope and decomposition. The reference FLA implementation (Yang & Zhang, 2024) targets general training and inference settings, supporting variable head dimensions, sequence lengths, recurrent states, backward propagation, and final-state outputs. In contrast, our CUDA operator is specialized for GTR inference with batch size one, FP16 inputs, zero initial state, no backward propagation or final-state output, chunk size = 64, and per-head dimensions dk = 32 and dv = 64. As described in Section 2.1, GTR fixes the value-side state-decay gate to βt 11dv during both training and inference. Consequently, the training-time FLA kernels and our custom operator consume identical inputsQ, K, V, and the learned key-side log-decay gate gand evaluate the same recurrence. The data-dependent output gate is likewise preserved and may be fused into the deployment epilogue. Up to mixed-precision roundoff, our operator therefore changes only the execution schedule and fusion pattern, not the underlying computation. remaining inefficiency in FLA v0.5.0 is that each state-tile program processes chunks sequentially, performing matrix contraction at every step and exposing limited parallelism in our small-batch regime. Let Nc = L/C denote the number of chunks. We instead parallelize the expensive chunk summaries Uc in Equation 3 over the chunkhead grid, leaving only the lightweight boundary-state recurrence as sequential scan; adjacent lanes process adjacent elements along the contiguous dv dimension, enabling coalesced memory accesses. While tree-based prefix scan achieves O(log Nc) depth, it requires additional global-memory passes and strided accesses in our setting. We find the coalesced linear scan faster in the target deployment regime while still retaining O(L) work for fixed head dimensions and chunk size. Fused tensor-core dataflow. Building on this schedule, our first kernel fuses chunk-local cumulative sums with the construction of Uc. Prefix sums are computed in FP32 registers, while value tiles are staged in padded shared memory via cp.async. The fixed configuration = 64, dk = 32, dv = 64 maps efficiently to ldmatrix loads and tensor-core MMA instructions with FP32 accumulation: chunk-summary and scorevalue contractions use FP16 operands, whereas the decayrescaled query/key operands and boundary states use BF16 to accommodate their wider dynamic range. Kernel tiling and dispatch parameters are tuned for RTX 4090 sm 89. For each chunkhead pair, second kernel jointly computes the causal (cid:101)Q (cid:101)K scores, their product with V, and the boundary-state readout within single thread block. The resulting 64 64 causal score tile is consumed directly from shared memory rather than materialized to global memory, eliminating the standalone cumulative-sum launch and an intermediate intra-chunk score tensor of size O(LHC). Chunk-local cumulative sums are still exchanged between the summary and output kernels through an FP16 workspace. Length-aware scheduling and deployment fusion. Because the relative cost of the scan and output stages depends on Nc, we adopt length-aware dispatch policy. For short sequences, fallback output kernel reconstructs chunk prefixes inline, avoiding separate scan launch; under our default RTX 4090 dispatch policy, this path is used for Nc < 6. For eligible non-wave-aligned grids with Nc 6, an occupancy-aware kernel instead combines the scan and output stages: output blocks compute the chunk-local contractions while scan blocks generate boundary states, with synchroA18 Figure 8: Qualitative object detection results of GTR-X. nization occurring only immediately before the boundary-state readout so that the two stages can overlap. All other configurations retain separate scan kernel. Beyond kernel scheduling, the deployment interface supports persistent caller-managed workspaces, preallocated output buffers, and CUDA Graph capture. In the end-to-end GTR implementation, the output epilogue further fuses RMSNorm and the SiLU-activated output gatedistinct from the subsequent S-SwiGLU channel mixerdirectly into the GLA kernel, removing one kernel launch and its intermediate global-memory round trip. This epilogue fusion is excluded from the isolated operator measurements in Figure 4.

sections.title: F QUALITATIVE RESULTS
sections.content: We present qualitative results for object detection, instance segmentation, human pose estimation, semantic segmentation, zero-shot monocular depth estimation, and oriented object detection. The COCO examples include occlusion, low illumination, motion blur, defocus, object rotation, and crowded scenes. The additional transfer examples use Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016) for semantic segmentation, the DTU Robot Image Data Set (Jensen et al., 2014) for indoor depth, nuScenes (Caesar et al., 2020) for outdoor depth, and the DOTA-v1.0 (Xia et al., 2018) test set for oriented object detection. F.1 OBJECT DETECTION RESULTS Detection behavior. Figure 8 illustrates selected GTR-X predictions under crowding and occlusion, motion blur, object rotation, and low illumination. Across these examples, the model localizes small and overlapping instances despite substantial appearance degradation. F.2 INSTANCE SEGMENTATION RESULTS Mask quality. Figure 9 visualizes GTR-X masks on the same challenging images as Figure 8. The selected predictions follow visible object contours and separate adjacent instances; together with Table 8, they illustrate the transfer of the output-aligned representation to instance segmentation. A19 Figure 9: Qualitative instance segmentation results of GTR-X. Predictions are visualized on the same image set used in Figure 8. Figure 10: Qualitative human pose estimation results of GTR-X. The examples emphasize crowded scenes, low illumination, and motion blur. F.3 HUMAN POSE ESTIMATION RESULTS Pose behavior. The selected cases in Figure 10 show GTR-X predicting articulated poses for multiple overlapping people under crowding, low illumination, and motion blur. Figure 11: Qualitative semantic segmentation results of GTR-X. Each row shows, from left to right, the input RGB image, GTR-X prediction, and ground-truth annotation. F.4 SEMANTIC SEGMENTATION RESULTS Dense semantic predictions. Figure 11 compares GTR-X predictions with Cityscapes ground truth. F.5 ZERO-SHOT MONOCULAR DEPTH ESTIMATION RESULTS We apply GTR-L without dataset-specific fine-tuning to indoor DTU and outdoor nuScenes imagery. F.5. INDOOR DTU RESULTS Projected reference depth. For these examples, DTU provides calibrated point-cloud geometry rather than dense per-view depth maps. We therefore construct reference depth by projecting the point cloud through each camera using the provided intrinsics and calibrated pose. The resulting reference maps cover 67.9% of pixels on average; missing support is concentrated in the background fabric, which was not captured by structured light, and on specular surfaces. Figure 12 compares the RGB inputs, GTR-L predictions, and projected references. Depth-based reconstruction. Figure 13 visualizes reconstructions obtained from all 49 calibrated views of each DTU object. Since single image does not geometrically determine absolute depth scale, depth maps predicted independently across views may exhibit view-dependent scale drift. Prior to fusion, we therefore align the scale of each predicted depth map using single scalar, computed as the median ratio between the projected structured-light reference depth and the prediction over valid pixels. This per-view rescaling preserves the relative depth structure within each view while correcting only its global scale. We then back-project the rescaled depth maps using the calibrated camera intrinsics and extrinsics, fuse all 49 views into TSDF (Curless & Levoy, 1996) volume with 2-mm voxels, and render the resulting surface as colored points. Because the structured-light reference supplies one global scale factor per view, these reconstructions illustrate the geometry after reference-assisted scale correction. Figures 1416 show GTR-L predictions for the six synchronized surroundview cameras in three nuScenes scenes. Each figure preserves the camera ordering between the RGB grid and the corresponding depth grid, covering daytime, nighttime, and roadside construction imagery without nuScenes-specific fine-tuning. Temporally fused local maps. To visualize multi-frame geometric consistency, for each reference time t, we aggregate all available frames within [t 4 s, + 4 s]. For each frame, we scale-align the GTR-L depth prediction using single scalar estimated from the corresponding LiDAR measurements, back-project the corrected depth with the camera intrinsics, and transform the resulting points into common coordinate frame using the calibrated pose. We then fuse all observations with TSDF (Curless & Levoy, 1996) to obtain local map. Figures 17 and 18 show two examples from perspective and birds-eye views. Since LiDAR is used only for per-frame scale alignment, these results qualitatively illustrate geometric consistency after scale correction.
